question: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Petr Bystron (ESN), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Mathilde Androuët (PfE), Laurence Trochu (ECR), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Laurent Castillo (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), António Tânger Corrêa (PfE), Annamária Vicsek (PfE), András Gyürk (PfE), György Hölvényi (PfE), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE) Subject:

Presented as an instrument of academic excellence and international university cooperation, the Erasmus Mundus programme provides funding for third-country nationals to come to the EU, as well as partnerships with institutions outside the EU. Against a backdrop of high budgetary tensions and migratory pressures, and with some universities being entry routes to European territory, this policy raises legitimate questions. In addition, a series of controversies relating to the funding of problematic institutions mean there is a call for greater transparency. 1.

Can the Commission specify the proportion of third-country nationals among the beneficiaries of the Erasmus Mundus programme, which countries they come from, and the total amount of funding allocated to them?
Does it monitor what becomes of the beneficiaries after their studies, in particular in the event that they stay in the EU, abandon their studies or abuse the initial purpose of stay?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) International students contribute to the EU’s economy by filling skill gaps, driving research and innovation, and contributing to a more skilled workforce. The Erasmus Mundus action is designed to attract talent, promote academic excellence, international cooperation, and the attractiveness of European higher education. It supports high-quality joint master’s programmes delivered by consortia of higher education institutions, with scholarships awarded to the best students worldwide on the basis of excellence and equal treatment principles1. Third-country nationals are selected from a wide range of countries across the world. The selection and decision to award the grants is done by the joint master’s, following the programme’s guidelines. Since 2004, a total of 41 474 students have benefited of Erasmus Mundus scholarships, of which 35 826 (86%) were non-EU nationals. The top five non-EU nationalities of scholarship holders since 2004 are India, China, Brazil, Pakistan and Mexico. The proportion of non-EU nationals awarded an Erasmus Mundus scholarship varies yearly; in 2025 it was of 81%, with an amount of EUR 65 million devoted to scholarships for this group to participate in joint programmes that typically last for two years. Erasmus Mundus mobility is subject to the applicable EU and national legal frameworks, including on visa and residence, in particular Directive (EU) 2016/8012. The Commission monitors the implementation of the programme, including participation and completion data, through the Erasmus+ performance and reporting framework. Decisions on the right of residence after the completion of the studies and the enforcement of migration rules remain primarily within the competence of Member States.
